explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Peter urges them to abstain from the desires of the flesh, “…which war against your soul.” (1 Peter 2:11) Notice what's fighting here: those desires are the ones going after your soul. Warm dough has picked a few fights with me too, and I only won some of them.

I see why you'd go there, since the Gentiles start slandering them in the very next verse. But in verse 11 Peter names something else. He says the desires of the flesh are what war against the soul. Fear of people never shows up in that line, friend.

Foreigners and exiles sure have plenty of troubles, I'll give you that. But Peter says it's the desires of the flesh that war against their soul. Those are what he tells them to abstain from. You can't abstain from a flat tire, friend, but you can say no to a desire.

Peter doesn't say that anywhere, friend. He tells the believers to conduct themselves with such honor that the slanderers may see their good deeds. Slander gets answered with honor, not with more slander. Throwing it back would be the easy road, and Peter doesn't take it.

False, and you read it right. Peter says to conduct yourselves with such honor among the Gentiles that, though they slander you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God. So the answer to slander is honor and good deeds. That's a hard road, friend, and a road Peter says to walk.
Glorify, friend! The slanderers see the good deeds and glorify God. Peter says it happens “…on the day He visits us.” (1 Peter 2:12) Good deeds do the talking, and God gets the glory.

Blame is what slanderers are busy handing out, so I get the pull. But Peter says that when they see the good deeds, they glorify God. The word in that blank turns the whole verse upside down. Blame is out and glory is in.

Forget isn't in this verse at all, friend. Peter says the people slandering them see the good deeds and glorify God. They're looking right at something worth noticing. The day Peter names is the day He visits us.
The Lord, friend. Peter says to submit “…for the Lord’s sake to every human institution…” (1 Peter 2:13) The reason he gives is the Lord. That changes how a believer follows the rules.
That's a natural guess, since institutions are made of people. But Peter says to submit for the Lord's sake. He doesn't say for people's sake. Same instruction, different reason, friend.

Close to the neighborhood, since Peter does mention the king and governors. But the verse says to submit for the Lord's sake, not the nation's. The Lord is the reason Peter gives. I'd love to give you partial credit for effort, friend.

That's it, friend. Peter says the governors are sent by the king “…to punish those who do wrong and to praise those who do right.” (1 Peter 2:14) Two jobs, and they go in both directions. Doing right gets praise, and that's right there in the text.

Taxes and roads sound like governor work to us, I know. But Peter doesn't mention either one here. He says the governors are sent to punish those who do wrong and to praise those who do right. I'll stick to what the verse says, friend.

explanations.answer: Guard the borders of the land
explanations.explanation: Borders would be a big job, no doubt. But Peter never brings up borders in this passage. The governors are sent to punish those who do wrong and to praise those who do right. Those are the only two jobs he names.

By doing good, friend. Peter says it's God's will that “…by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish men.” (1 Peter 2:15) Good deeds are the whole plan. A quiet life of good outlasts a loud argument.

Sneaky one, since the verse does say silence. But the believers aren't told to go quiet. They're told to do good, and that's what silences the ignorance. The silence is the result, friend, not the method.
Packing up sounds tempting some days. But Peter never tells them to move. He says doing good is how the ignorance of foolish men gets silenced. They stay put and do good.
True! Peter says, “Live in freedom, but do not use your freedom as a cover-up for evil…” (1 Peter 2:16) Freedom is a gift, and it isn't a hiding spot. You've got that one down, friend.

It's actually True, friend. Peter does warn them: “Live in freedom, but do not use your freedom as a cover-up for evil…” (1 Peter 2:16) Freedom is real, and it's not meant to hide evil behind. The warning is right there in the verse.
Servants, friend! Peter says to live free, “…live as servants of God.” (1 Peter 2:16) Free and serving go together in this verse. Freedom without a cover-up means living as God's servants.
Rulers sounds like a promotion, I know. But Peter says to live as servants of God. Freedom here isn't about taking charge. It's about who you serve, friend.
Judges, huh? Peter says no such thing about the believers. He tells them to live as servants of God. Judging is not the job being handed out in this verse, friend.
The king, friend. Peter's short line says, “Love the brotherhood of believers, fear God, honor the king.” (1 Peter 2:17) Three commands, each with its own target. Honor goes to the king.

Elders are a fair guess, since honor is the kind of thing you'd give them. But in this line Peter doesn't name them. He says, “Love the brotherhood of believers, fear God, honor the king.” (1 Peter 2:17) The king is the one who gets the honor here.
Priests do sound like honor material. But in this line Peter doesn't name them. He says to love the brotherhood of believers, fear God, and honor the king. The king is the one named, friend.

Unreasonable, friend! Peter says to submit “…not only to those who are good and gentle, but even to those who are unreasonable.” (1 Peter 2:18) The word even is doing heavy lifting there. It isn't only the easy bosses.

Foreign is a sensible guess, since Peter calls the believers foreigners and exiles. But when he names the other masters, he says unreasonable ones. Peter is talking about how a master treats people, not where he's from. That's the contrast with good and gentle, friend.

Former masters would be a surprising twist, but it's not in the verse. Peter says to submit to the good and gentle, “…but even to those who are unreasonable.” (1 Peter 2:18) The contrast is about how a master acts. Not when he was the master, friend.

True, friend. Peter says, “For if anyone endures the pain of unjust suffering because he is conscious of God, this is to be commended.” (1 Peter 2:19) It's pain nobody had coming, and Peter still calls it commendable. You nailed it.

It's actually True, friend. Peter says it right there: “For if anyone endures the pain of unjust suffering because he is conscious of God, this is to be commended.” (1 Peter 2:19) Commended is the word he uses. I'll hand you a fresh sheet of dough for the next one.

That's it, friend. Peter says, “But if you suffer for doing good and you endure it, this is commendable before God.” (1 Peter 2:20) He sets it right beside being beaten for doing wrong. Good deeds put you in the commendable column.

Years of suffering sounds like it would earn a medal. But Peter never mentions how long. He says suffering for doing good and enduring it is commendable before God. The length isn't the point, friend, the reason is.

Nice try, but secrets don't show up in this verse. Peter's contrast is between being beaten for doing wrong and suffering for doing good. The one he calls commendable before God is the suffering for doing good. Whether anybody knows isn't the question, friend.

An example, friend! Peter says Christ suffered for you, “…leaving you an example, that you should follow in His footsteps…” (1 Peter 2:21) He left a trail to follow. That's what the next verses lay out.

A warning would be a heavy thing to leave behind. But Peter says Christ left an example. He suffered for them, and they can follow in His footsteps. Footsteps are something you walk in, friend, not something you flinch from.

Laws are a fair guess, since people often think of rules first. But Peter says Christ left an example, so that they should follow in His footsteps. The picture is walking behind someone, not reading a rulebook. Footsteps, friend.
True, friend. Peter quotes it: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth.” (1 Peter 2:22) No sin, and no deceit in His mouth. That's the One whose footsteps they're told to follow.

It's True, friend. Peter says of Jesus, “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth.” (1 Peter 2:22) Nothing is hiding in His record. I'll have a quiet word with this one later, but you're right on track.

The text says the opposite, friend. Peter says, “When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate…” (1 Peter 2:23) Abuse came His way, and He didn't hit back. That's the example Peter is holding up.

False, and you've got it. Peter says, “When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats…” (1 Peter 2:23) No retaliation and no threats. That's a lot of strength, friend, and I think it takes more than I've got.
Justly, friend. Peter says Jesus “…entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly.” (1 Peter 2:23) He didn't make threats. He put Himself in the hands of the One who judges justly.
Quickly makes sense if you're in pain and want it over with. But Peter says the One who judges does it justly. Speed isn't mentioned in the verse. Justly is the word, friend.
Gently is a sweet word, but it's not the one Peter uses here. He says Jesus entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly. That's the word that went in the blank. Justly, friend.

Die, friend. Peter says Jesus bore our sins in His body on the tree “…so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.” (1 Peter 2:24) Dying to sin and living to righteousness go together in one sentence. I can't say it's easy, but I can say that's the plan in the text.

Return does show up in this passage, but later, in verse 25, where the believers have returned to the Shepherd. In verse 24 the word is die. Peter says Jesus bore our sins so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. Right passage, wrong verse, friend.

Cling is a reasonable-sounding word, but Peter doesn't use it. He says Jesus bore our sins so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. Sin is something we die to, not something we hold onto, friend.

Shepherd, friend! Peter says, “For ‘you were like sheep going astray,’ but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.” (1 Peter 2:25) Sheep going astray, then back to the Shepherd. That's a good place to land at the end.

King does come up in this passage, back in verse 17, where Peter says to honor the king. But this verse names the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls. Sheep go with a Shepherd, friend. Easy to mix up since Peter packs a lot in.

Priest sounds like a title that fits the moment. But Peter says the believers returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls. With the sheep picture right there, Shepherd is the one that matches. Nice try, friend.
